title: Holding Up the Minor Voice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that meeting leaders must commit to holding up the minor voice, meaning everyone, including reticent, inexperienced or introverted people, is heard. The author ties this to decision quality, which depends on having all views on the table. Three tactics are offered: ask habitually silent members for their views before the meeting, call on people by name during it, and remind non-contributors of their obligation afterward. Previewing a viewpoint and praising it beforehand makes it easier for the person to voice it in the room. The underlying move is to establish a norm that every member will be asked and expected to contribute. The piece ends by asking how many team members engage passively and urging leaders to get them heard.
points: Decision quality depends on everyone's view, so leaders must deliberately draw out quiet team members.
Pre-meeting conversations let a leader hear and praise a quiet person's idea so it is easier to share in the room.
Calling on people by name and never leaving a topic without hearing from everyone creates a norm of contribution.
Follow-up after the meeting reminds silent members that participation is an obligation, not an option.
quotes: Translated, this means to make sure everyone is heard and contributes to the discussion. This includes those who are reticent, inexperienced, introverted, or fearful of interjecting their views.

Decision quality depends on everyone’s view. Making sure all opinions are on the table before landing on a decision or conclusion is essential work. But getting the quiet types to speak up is not always easy.
Good leaders have learned a few tricks along the way. Prior to the meeting, they will ask those with a pattern of meeting silence for their views on the topics to be discussed.

Another important strategy for getting others to talk is for the leader to call on them during the meeting: “Terry, what’s your view on this?” Making the commitment not to leave a topic or meeting without hearing from every team member creates the norm for contribution.

When team members know they will be asked their opinion, and have little choice but to offer it, they learn to speak up without prompting. Good leaders don’t hesitate to call for a viewpoint from those who haven’t spoken.

By suggesting all team members have an obligation to contribute and offer their candid views, leaders set the proper expectations for participation. On good teams, no one is allowed to sit like a potted plant and just watch the action. Everyone is expected to contribute.
